title: Twenty-Three Words: the Minister, the Premium Department, and the Pledge That Outlived Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mount Morris, birth in the manse
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate is Mount Morris town centre, the church site itself unconfirmed
stops.campa: In the Genesee valley village of Mount Morris a son is born to David Bellamy, minister of the First Baptist Church, and to Lucy Clark Bellamy. They name him Francis Julius. The house he is born into runs on the week of a country pastorate: sermon, visitation, the Sunday oath of the congregation renewed. The working vocabulary of that house is covenant and the pledged word, allegiance sworn aloud in a room full of people on their feet. Thirty-seven years later a nation of schoolchildren will stand each morning and say twenty-three words he wrote.
suggested_refs: The First Baptist Church of Mount Morris, David Bellamy's pastorate at the time of his son's birth
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Rome, the family moves to the First Baptist Church
stops.date_confidence: Little Falls Historical Society gives 1859, on David Bellamy's acceptance of the Rome pastorate; Wikipedia says the boy was about five, implying 1860; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: David Bellamy accepts the pastorate of the First Baptist Church of Rome, on the Erie Canal in Oneida County, and moves the household east. Francis is four. Rome will hold his father's pulpit, his schooling, his baptism, and the ground his ashes are carried back to from Florida seventy-two years on. He grows up a canal-town boy in the decade before the war, in a denomination that argues about slavery every Sunday and settles it in no year that he is old enough to remember.
suggested_refs: The First Baptist Church of Rome, W. Embargo Street, the church of Bellamy's boyhood
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Rome, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; the October dating and the place of death come from the Little Falls Historical Society and are reconstruction
stops.campa: David Bellamy dies with the war still running. Francis is nine. The widow keeps the family in Rome and the congregation keeps the family in view, and the vocation passes to the boy the way a trade passes in a workshop, by proximity rather than by any decision anyone records. He will be ordained at twenty-four into his father's denomination and his father's state, preaching from his father's book. What he does with the pulpit once he has it will take it away from him for good.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives record of David Bellamy's death at Rome
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Rome, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested with day precision by the Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives
stops.campa: At thirteen Francis Bellamy is baptized in the church his father served, five years after burying him. Baptist baptism is not administered to infants; it waits for a person old enough to answer for the answer. He goes into the water having decided, and comes out of it a member of the body that raised him. It is the first oath of his life that he takes in his own voice, in front of witnesses, in a room where the ceremony is the whole of the meaning. The sentence he writes at thirty-seven asks a room of children to do the same thing at a signal from the principal.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the First Baptist Church of Rome, 7 March 1869
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Rochester, the university on Prince Street
stops.date_confidence: class of 1876 per the Little Falls Historical Society, implying entry in 1872; other summaries give attendance as c.1873-1877; month is a convention
stops.campa: He graduates from the Rome Free Academy and goes west along the canal to the University of Rochester, whose campus then stands on Prince Street. He reads theology and joins Alpha Delta Phi, and takes his degree in 1876 at twenty-one. The Academy building of 1872 cannot now be located and the Prince Street campus is gone, its ground occupied by an art gallery, so the geography of his education survives as two addresses that no longer hold what happened at them. What the record keeps of those four years is a degree and two entry dates that do not agree.
suggested_refs: The Prince Street campus of the University of Rochester, now the site of the Memorial Art Gallery, 500 University Avenue
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Rochester, the theological seminary
stops.date_confidence: completion given as 1879 by the Little Falls Historical Society and as 1880 by Britannica; the December 1879 ordination favours 1879; the conflict is not resolved and the month is a convention
stops.campa: He stays in Rochester for the Rochester Theological Seminary, three years of Hebrew, homiletics, and the pastoral care of congregations he does not yet have. The seminary is a Baptist house in a burnt-over district, downstream of two generations of revival and reform, and the social gospel is arriving in it while he sits there. He comes out of it in 1879 able to build a sermon the way an engineer builds a truss, and with the conviction, not yet dangerous to him, that the teachings of Jesus have economic content.
suggested_refs: The Rochester Theological Seminary, later merged into Colgate Rochester Crozer Divinity School
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Little Falls, lodging at the Girvan House
stops.date_confidence: the Cooney Archives date the lodging to 1879-1880 without a month; November is inferred from the pastorate beginning 1 December
stops.campa: He arrives at Little Falls, a mill town in the Mohawk gorge where the canal drops forty feet through locks, and takes a room at the Girvan House on West Main Street. He is twenty-four, unmarried, and about to be handed a church with a six-thousand-dollar debt. The building will become the Snyder Apartments; the lodging is recorded because a local historical society kept the kind of record that national encyclopedias do not. Almost everything precise that is known about this life comes from towns of this size keeping books on their own.
suggested_refs: The Girvan House, 2-8 West Main Street, Little Falls, now the Snyder Apartments
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: First Baptist Church, Little Falls, the first pastorate
stops.date_confidence: attested with day precision by the Little Falls Historical Society; the coordinate is the Albany Street church, whose present building postdates his tenure
stops.campa: On the first of December he accepts the pastorate of the First Baptist Church of Little Falls, his first. He will hold it five years and two months. In that time the congregation clears a debt of six thousand dollars, a sum that in a mill town is raised a dollar at a time from people who work in the mills. The church he preached in is not the building that stands on Albany Street now; the present one was raised in 1895, after he had gone to Boston and after the pledge, and the plaque it will hang for him is eighty-four years off.
suggested_refs: The First Baptist Church of Little Falls, 549 Albany Street; the 1895 building replaced the one Bellamy preached in
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: First Baptist Church, Little Falls, the ordination
stops.date_confidence: attested with day precision by the Little Falls Historical Society; other sources round to 1879 or 1880
stops.campa: Two weeks into the pastorate the council lays hands on him and he is ordained a Baptist minister. He is the son of a Baptist minister, ordained into the same order, in the same state, fifteen years after his father's funeral. Other sources round the day away and say only 1879, or say 1880; the town that watched it happen wrote down the fourteenth of December. He is now, in the language of the denomination, a man set apart, and the setting apart is done by a room of people agreeing out loud.
suggested_refs: The ordination council record of 14 December 1879, Cooney Archives
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Newark, the marriage to Harriet Benton
stops.date_confidence: Little Falls Historical Society gives 1 June 1880 at Newark; Wikipedia gives 1881; the conflict is not resolved; the coordinate is Newark town centre, the church of the ceremony unconfirmed
stops.campa: Six months into his first church he marries Harriet Benton at Newark, in Wayne County, west along the canal. The national account of his life gives the year as 1881 and no day and no place; the county record gives the first of June 1880, and gives the town. Both are printed and neither has been withdrawn. They will be married thirty-eight years, will have three sons and perhaps four children, and she will die in New York in a November when he is sixty-three and has been out of the ministry for a quarter of a century.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives marriage record, Newark, New York, 1 June 1880
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: 25 Alexander Street, eighty dollars in gold
stops.date_confidence: attested with day precision by the Little Falls Historical Society; the common gloss tying the gift to the retirement of the church debt is a conflation and is not made here
stops.campa: On the fifth of January congregants leave eighty dollars in gold at the Bellamy house on Alexander Street, anonymously, the way a mill town thanks a man it cannot pay properly. In the house is a son, John Benton, born at Newark the September before. The gift is often told as the congregation's thanks for clearing a six-thousand-dollar debt; the debt was cleared across the whole pastorate and the archive does not tie the two together. What is recorded is the date, the metal, and that nobody signed it.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives entry for 5 January 1883; the Bellamy residence at 25 Alexander Street
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Little Falls, the departure for Boston
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Little Falls Historical Society
stops.campa: On the first of February he leaves the Mohawk gorge for a Boston pulpit. He is twenty-nine, with a wife, a son, a debt-free church behind him, and a reputation as a preacher who can fill a room. Boston in 1885 is where the American social gospel is loudest and where Christian socialism is about to acquire an organization, a magazine, and a membership list. Everything that makes him famous and everything that ends his ministry is waiting there, and the two turn out to be the same six years.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives record of the pastorate's end, 1 February 1885
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

segments.name: Boston: Two Pulpits and the Christian Socialists

stops.name: Dearborn Street Baptist Church, the Roxbury pulpit
stops.date_confidence: year and month attested by the Little Falls Historical Society; the coordinate is approximate, the street address of the building not located
stops.campa: He takes the pulpit of the Dearborn Street Baptist Church in Roxbury and holds it five years. Boston is a city of textile capital and Irish labour and a Brahmin philanthropy that prefers charity to arithmetic, and Bellamy preaches arithmetic. He argues from the Gospels that the distribution of economic resources is a religious question and that the working man's claim on it is not a matter of alms. The congregation is patient for a while. The record does not preserve his sermons; it preserves what the sermons cost him.
suggested_refs: The Dearborn Street Baptist Church, Roxbury, Bellamy's pulpit 1885 to 1890
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Liberty Island, the other civic icon is dedicated
stops.date_confidence: the dedication is attested; no source places Bellamy at it, and this stop is context rather than an attested presence
stops.campa: In New York harbour a copper woman on an iron armature is unveiled before a fleet and a President. The armature inside her is the work of Gustave Eiffel, who three years later will raise a tower in Paris on the same principles. She is the republic made into an object that a crowd can face and take off its hat to. Six years later Bellamy will supply the words for a different object, cheap and reproducible, hoisted on a pole in twenty-six thousand schoolyards. No source places him at this ceremony. The two devices belong to one decade.
suggested_refs: The dedication of the Statue of Liberty, 28 October 1886; Eiffel's internal armature

stops.name: Roxbury, the birth of David Bellamy
stops.date_confidence: attested with day precision by the Little Falls Historical Society
stops.campa: A second son, David, is born at Roxbury. John is six. A third son will come in 1896 and die in infancy, which corrects the usual telling: the child who died was the youngest, not the eldest. One genealogical record counts four children rather than three, and the national account gives no dates for any of them, so the family that a schoolroom sentence was written inside is documented worse than the sentence. In January of the coming year their father will help found a socialist society and put his name to it as an officer.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives birth record for David Bellamy, Roxbury, 30 October 1888
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Tremont Temple, the Society of Christian Socialists founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Wikipedia's article on the Society; the coordinate for Tremont Temple, 88 Tremont Street, is geocoded here and is not supplied by the source
stops.campa: Nineteen men meet at Tremont Temple and found the Society of Christian Socialists: the Episcopal priest W. D. P. Bliss, A. G. Lawson, Bellamy, and sixteen others. Bellamy is made founding vice president. Their claim is simple and, to a Boston congregation paying his salary, intolerable: that the economic teaching of Jesus is socialism and that the church has been reading around it. His cousin Edward Bellamy has published Looking Backward the year before and has a movement of his own. William Morris is preaching the same decade in London.
suggested_refs: Tremont Temple, 88 Tremont Street, Boston, founding meeting of 18 February 1889

stops.name: Boston, the Society takes its form
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: declaration of principles 15 April, constitution 24 April, permanent organization 7 May, first issue of The Dawn 15 May 1889
stops.campa: In nine weeks the Society acquires everything an institution needs. A declaration of principles on the fifteenth of April, a constitution on the twenty-fourth, permanent organization on the seventh of May, and on the fifteenth the first issue of its magazine, The Dawn. Branches open in New York by February, then Ohio, Illinois, and Kansas by August of 1890. The current is transatlantic: Annie Besant is moving through Fabian rooms in London the same years, and the argument they are all downstream of was written by Karl Marx in Paris in 1843.
suggested_refs: The Dawn, magazine of the Society of Christian Socialists, first issue 15 May 1889

stops.name: Bethany Baptist Church, the last pastorate
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Little Falls Historical Society, month unknown and defaulted; the coordinate is approximate, the address not located
stops.campa: He leaves Dearborn Street and takes Bethany Baptist Church, in Boston, his last pastorate. He is thirty-four and an officer of a socialist society whose membership list is public. Accounts that put his ejection at Dearborn Street are wrong by one church: he is at Bethany from 1890, and it is Bethany that he goes out of. The exact address of the building has not been recovered by anyone who wrote about him, which is a way of saying that the church that ended his career is now a coordinate with an error bar.
suggested_refs: Bethany Baptist Church, Boston, Bellamy's final pulpit
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Bethany Baptist Church, out of the pulpit
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted; Wikipedia says he was forced out for preaching against the evils of capitalism, a secondary summary says he stepped away as his convictions diverged from the congregation, and the two framings are not reconciled
stops.campa: In 1891 the pulpit closes behind him. One account says he was forced out for preaching against the evils of capitalism; another says he stepped away as his convictions drifted past what the congregation would carry. Twelve years of ministry end and he does not enter another. In New York, Felix Adler has already built the alternative that Bellamy will now improvise for himself: civic and moral ritual detached from doctrine. Bellamy detaches it not into a society of ethics but into a magazine's premium department.
suggested_refs: The 1891 departure from Bethany Baptist Church, Boston

stops.name: Boston, Daniel Sharp Ford hires him
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted; the coordinate is the Columbus Avenue building of 1892, which postdates the hiring, and the magazine's address at that moment is an open gap
stops.campa: Daniel Sharp Ford, owner of The Youth's Companion, takes the unemployed minister onto his staff and sets him to work in the premium department alongside Ford's nephew, James B. Upham. The common telling makes Upham the employer; Ford hired him, Upham was the colleague. The Companion is the largest-circulation magazine in the country, sold by subscription and paid for partly in premiums, and the premium the department is currently pushing into American schools is the flag. Bellamy has gone from preaching a republic to merchandising one.
suggested_refs: The Youth's Companion Building, 209 Columbus Avenue, Boston, occupied from 1892

stops.name: Boston, twenty-six thousand flags
stops.date_confidence: the 26,000 figure is attested for 1892 and the campaign's start for 1888; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: The campaign began in 1888: a school that sold enough subscriptions received a flag. By 1892 some twenty-six thousand public schools have taken one. A commercial premium scheme has quietly installed the national emblem in the daily life of the American schoolroom, and the emblem now needs something for the children to do in front of it. The department that supplied the object is asked to supply the ceremony. The liturgy of American citizenship is commissioned by a circulation department.
suggested_refs: The Youth's Companion school flag premium campaign, 1888 onward

stops.name: Saratoga Springs, the National Council of Education endorses the programme
stops.date_confidence: the endorsement is attested via the Journal of Education, June 1892, relayed in secondary aggregation; Bellamy's personal attendance is reconstruction, and the day is unknown
stops.campa: The National Council of Education, meeting at Saratoga Springs, endorses the Columbus Day school programme that Bellamy has chaired the committee to prepare. With that vote a magazine's marketing idea becomes an educational proposal with professional standing behind it, and the four hundredth anniversary of the landfall acquires a national classroom ceremony. Whether Bellamy is in the room is not established by any accessible source; that he chaired the committee is. The endorsement travels; the man may not have.
suggested_refs: Journal of Education, June 1892, on the National Council of Education at Saratoga
sources: Journal of Education (June 1892), via secondary aggregation
masonicworld.com summary (relayed; the page itself returned HTTP 403)

stops.name: Boston, the writing of the Pledge
stops.date_confidence: August 1892 is the conventional dating of the composition; no source in the pool gives a day
stops.campa: He writes it in the magazine's offices, built to be spoken in about fifteen seconds by a room of children. He starts from allegiance and works outward, choosing pledge over vow and swear as the better school word, choosing the first person singular, choosing my flag over the flag. He leaves God out. A Baptist minister composing the central ritual sentence of American civic life declines to name God in it, and says later that the true reason for allegiance to the flag is the republic for which it stands.
stops.quote: Beginning with the new word allegiance, I first decided that 'pledge' was a better school word than 'vow' or 'swear'; and that the first person singular should be used, and that 'my' flag was preferable to 'the.'
stops.quote_source: Francis Bellamy, quoted in the Congressional Record, 91 Cong. Rec. (1945), House, pp. 5510-5511
suggested_refs: Bellamy's own account of the composition, entered into the Congressional Record in 1945
sources: Congressional Record, 91 Cong. Rec. (1945), House, pp. 5510-5511

stops.name: Boston, the Pledge is printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; sources disagree on the punctuation and capitalisation of the 1892 printing, and the variant reproduced on Wikipedia reads 'I pledge Allegiance to my Flag and to the Republic for which it stands, one Nation indivisible, with Liberty and Justice for all'
stops.campa: The eighth of September issue carries the pledge, unsigned, among the instructions for the National School Celebration. Twenty-three words. No author's name is printed beside them, which is the ordinary practice of a premium department and the beginning of a century of argument about who wrote them. What is printed alongside is the choreography: pupils in ordered ranks, hands at the side, facing the flag at a signal from the principal, and the salute at the words, and the hands dropping.
stops.quote: I pledge allegiance to my Flag and the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
stops.quote_source: The Youth's Companion, 8 September 1892, as reproduced by ushistory.org
suggested_refs: The Youth's Companion issue of 8 September 1892, first printing of the Pledge

stops.name: Jackson Park, the Exposition dedicated
stops.date_confidence: the dedication date is attested; Bellamy's presence in Chicago is not established by any accessible source and this stop is reconstruction
stops.campa: At Jackson Park the World's Columbian Exposition is dedicated in the Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, the largest roofed room on earth, four hundred years and some calendar arithmetic after Columbus made his landfall. The following spring Eadweard Muybridge will open his Zoopraxographical Hall on the Midway and sell tickets to moving pictures of horses. Twelve years on, Max Weber will walk the same kind of fairground at St. Louis. No source puts Bellamy in Chicago. His sentence is being said in every state that day.
suggested_refs: The Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, Jackson Park, dedication of 21 October 1892

stops.name: Boston, ten thousand children and the raised arm
stops.date_confidence: attested; the observance was moved by President Harrison from 12 to 21 October to account for the 1752 Julian to Gregorian shift, and the 12 October date sometimes given is superseded
stops.campa: Under a proclamation of President Benjamin Harrison, more than ten thousand children say the verse together for the first National School Celebration, coordinated out of a Boston magazine office. They say it with the gesture Upham invented, arm out toward the flag, palm down and then up, performed to Bellamy's printed instructions. It becomes known as the Bellamy salute although Bellamy did not devise it. Mikhail Bakunin, sixteen years dead, had spent his life arguing that nothing whatever should bind a citizenry in this manner.
suggested_refs: Harrison's proclamation for the National School Celebration; Bellamy's printed ceremony instructions

stops.name: Boston, leaving the magazine
stops.date_confidence: the departure year is approximate, drawn from secondary aggregation rather than a primary biography; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He stays on the Companion's staff about four years past the pledge and leaves around 1896, the same year a third son is born who will not outlive infancy. He is forty-one, twice out of a career, and carries no public credit for the one sentence of his that the country now says out loud every morning. The departure year is an approximation from a secondary summary; nobody wrote the day down. From here the record of his life thins out for twenty years and does not thicken again until Tampa.
suggested_refs: The Youth's Companion staff records for the mid 1890s, not located
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: New York, the passage in The Illustrated American
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source consulted; The Illustrated American vol. XXII places it around 1897; the coordinate is generic Manhattan and carries no precision
stops.campa: In The Illustrated American he sets out what he thinks the republic can and cannot absorb. He divides immigrants by descent, welcoming those he calls akin to our own and their wholesome blood, and treats the rest as a danger to a country where every man is a lawmaker. The man who wrote liberty and justice for all wrote this too, in print, over his own name. Both statements stand unreconciled; the sentence the schoolchildren say does not know what its author thought about who should be saying it.
stops.quote: [a] democracy like ours cannot afford to throw itself open to the world where every man is a lawmaker, every dull-witted or fanatical immigrant admitted to our citizenship is a bane to the commonwealth.
stops.quote_source: Francis Bellamy, The Illustrated American, Vol. XXII, No. 394, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Francis Bellamy'
suggested_refs: The Illustrated American, Vol. XXII, No. 394; the adjacent passage on races akin to our own

stops.name: New York, the Erickson agency
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a secondary aggregation places him at Erickson 1916-1921, while Wikipedia's nineteen years in New York advertising implies roughly 1903-1922; the two chronologies conflict and are not resolved; the coordinate is the generic Midtown advertising district
stops.campa: He works as an account executive and copywriter for the Erickson Advertising Company. The former minister spends his sixties writing persuasion for hire, in the trade that had already trained him: the Companion's premium department was advertising with a schoolroom attached. How long the New York years ran is disputed. One count gives nineteen of them, another gives five at this agency, and no primary biography was reachable to settle it. The office address has not been recovered.
suggested_refs: The Erickson Advertising Company, New York, address not located

stops.name: New York, the death of Harriet Benton Bellamy
stops.date_confidence: day attested by the Little Falls Historical Society; Wikipedia gives only the year; the place of death is inferred from his residence and is not confirmed
stops.campa: Harriet Benton Bellamy dies on the third of November, thirty-eight years after Newark. The armistice is eight days away. The county archive that recorded their marriage records her death to the day; the national account gives 1918 and nothing else. Where she died is inferred from where he was living, which is the honest state of the evidence. He is sixty-three, a widower, and an advertising man, and the twenty-three words are being recited that morning in schools that have never heard his name.
suggested_refs: The Cooney Archives death record for Harriet Benton Bellamy, 3 November 1918
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: New York, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: the year 1920 is attested by both sources; the surname is not settled, Wikipedia giving Marie Morin and the Little Falls Historical Society giving Marie Marin; month, day, and place of the ceremony unknown
stops.campa: At sixty-five he marries again. Her given name is Marie and her surname is spelled two ways by the two sources that record her, Morin in the national account and Marin in the county archive, and no third source arbitrates. She will move with him to Florida in two years and be with him when he dies. A woman who shares the last eleven years of a life at the centre of American civic ritual is known to the record by a name that cannot be spelled with confidence.
suggested_refs: The 1920 marriage record, not located; the Morin and Marin spellings both in print
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Wallcraft Avenue, the move to Florida
stops.date_confidence: 1922 per Wikipedia, with one source giving 1924; month unknown and defaulted; the coordinate is the Bayshore end of West Wallcraft Avenue per OSM Nominatim, correcting a working value 1.7 km to the north
stops.campa: Bellamy and Marie move to Tampa and settle on Wallcraft Avenue, off Bayshore Boulevard, in a Florida in the middle of its land boom. He is sixty-seven. After the move he stops attending church altogether, which closes a line that ran from the Mount Morris manse through Rochester and two Boston pulpits and had been fraying for thirty years. One account gives 1924 rather than 1922 for the arrival. The street will one day carry a marker with his name and the word Pledge on it.
suggested_refs: West Wallcraft Avenue, South Tampa, near its Bayshore Boulevard end
sources: secondary aggregation citing the Tampa Tribune and historical marker text

stops.name: Washington, the National Flag Conference rewrites the line
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted; the change is two-step and is often collapsed into one, the 1923 conference substituting 'the Flag of the United States' for 'my Flag' and 'of America' being added in 1924
stops.campa: The National Flag Conference replaces my Flag with the Flag of the United States, and the following year adds of America. The stated reason is the foreign-born: a child from elsewhere saying my flag might, it is argued, mean another one. Bellamy is alive in Tampa, sixty-eight, and objects on the only ground he ever claimed for the sentence. He had chosen the possessive deliberately and counted the seconds it took to say. His objection is recorded, and disregarded, and the longer version is the one the country learns.
stops.quote: It did injure the rhythmic balance of the original composition.
stops.quote_source: Francis Bellamy on the 1923-24 revision, quoted in the Congressional Record, 91 Cong. Rec. (1945), House, pp. 5510-5511
suggested_refs: The National Flag Conference of 1923 and its 1924 sequel
sources: Congressional Record, 91 Cong. Rec. (1945), House, pp. 5510-5511

stops.name: Tampa Electric Company, advertising manager
stops.date_confidence: the 1926-1931 span is attested by Wikipedia; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He persuades the management of Tampa Electric that systematic publicity is worth paying for, and they hire him part-time to provide it. He is seventy-one. The last job of his life is writing copy for a utility in a boom town, five years of it, at the far end of a career that began with a Baptist ordination council laying hands on a young man in a Mohawk gorge. In those same years American schoolchildren recite his sentence every morning and no schoolbook prints his name under it.
suggested_refs: Tampa Electric Company records of the advertising department, 1926-1931

stops.name: Tampa Electric Company, the dismissal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Wikipedia
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July, in the second full year of the Depression, Tampa Electric lets him go. He is seventy-six and takes a position with the Tampa Gas Company instead. Six weeks remain to him. A man who was put out of a Boston pulpit for preaching that the economy was a religious question ends his working life cut from a utility payroll in a slump, and the day is on the record because a company kept books on its staff. In Tampa he is a gas company copywriter. The Pledge is thirty-nine years old, is recited that morning in every state, and carries no author's name.
suggested_refs: Tampa Gas Company, Bellamy's last employer

stops.name: Wallcraft Avenue, death at home
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the Wallcraft Avenue home, not the downtown Tampa Electric site sometimes given in error
stops.campa: Francis Bellamy dies at home on the twenty-eighth of August, aged seventy-six, six weeks after losing his job and a thousand miles from the church where he was baptized. Marie is with him. He has been out of the ministry forty years and away from the magazine thirty-five. The sentence he built to be spoken in fifteen seconds has by now been altered once without his consent, is performed with a raised arm he did not invent, and will be altered again twenty-three years after this morning.
suggested_refs: The Bellamy home on Wallcraft Avenue, South Tampa

stops.name: Rome Cemetery, the family plot on Jervis Avenue
stops.date_confidence: the burial year is attested and the cemetery identified by the Cooney Archives and a NYGenWeb transcription; the month is inferred from the death on 28 August; Find a Grave returned HTTP 403 and could not be consulted
stops.campa: His cremated remains go north to Rome and into the family plot at the cemetery on Jervis Avenue, seventy-two years after a four-year-old arrived in the town behind his father's call to the First Baptist Church. The national account says he was buried in the city where he was born, which is wrong: he was born at Mount Morris, sixty miles west. Rome is where he was raised, baptized, and buried, and it is the town that will hang a stained glass window with his twenty-three words in it.
suggested_refs: Rome Cemetery, Jervis Avenue, Rome, New York; the Bellamy family plot
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: Washington, the salute is legislated away
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Through the 1930s the extended arm of the schoolroom comes to look like the salute of Rome and Berlin, and interventionist propagandists photograph the isolationist Charles Lindbergh performing it from angles that crop the flag out of frame, so that the gesture appears to be the other one. On the twenty-second of December Congress passes Public Law 77-829 and replaces it with the hand over the heart. Upham's invention lasted fifty years and was named for a man who did not devise it and was eleven years dead when it was abolished.
suggested_refs: Public Law 77-829, 22 December 1942, amending the Flag Code

stops.name: Washington, under God
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; whether Bellamy would have accepted the change is not resolvable from the sources and is not asserted
stops.campa: On Flag Day, Congress inserts two words after one nation and President Eisenhower signs them, a Cold War amendment pressed by the Knights of Columbus to mark the republic off from state atheism. The Baptist minister who wrote the line had left God out on purpose, holding to the separation of church and state, and has been dead twenty-three years and cannot be asked. The sentence has now been edited twice by bodies he never sat on, and both edits were made in his name and against his stated preferences.
suggested_refs: The Flag Day amendment of 14 June 1954 adding 'under God'

stops.name: Little Falls, the Rev. Francis Bellamy Park dedicated
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Little Falls Historical Society; the streets named in that record, East Gansevoort, Burwell, and Salisbury, are all in Little Falls, correcting the frequent misattribution of this dedication to Rome, which has a separate Bellamy park beside its City Hall
stops.campa: The mill town of his first pastorate dedicates a park in his name at the meeting of East Gansevoort, Burwell, and Salisbury Streets, eighty years after the December when a council laid hands on him there. The dedication is often credited to Rome, which does have a Bellamy park of its own beside the City Hall, a separate one. Two towns claim him and both are entitled to: Rome raised and buried him, Little Falls ordained him and kept the only day-by-day record of his life that survives.
suggested_refs: Rev. Francis Bellamy Park, Little Falls, dedicated 12 September 1959
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: First Baptist Church, Little Falls, the plaque
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Little Falls Historical Society
stops.campa: The church fixes a plaque to mark the pastorate of 1879 to 1885. The building it hangs on is not the building he preached in; that one came down and the present church went up in 1895, so the plaque commemorates a ministry inside a structure that never held it. This is the ordinary condition of his geography. The Prince Street campus is an art gallery, the Academy of 1872 cannot be found, the Boston churches are approximate coordinates, and the offices where he wrote the pledge were demolished long ago.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque of 11 June 1963, First Baptist Church of Little Falls
sources: Little Falls Historical Society, Cooney Archives

stops.name: First Baptist Church, Rome, the window with the words in it
stops.date_confidence: no date: the source records the window without a year, and this date is a placeholder for ordering only and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: A member of the congregation designs a stained glass window for the church where Bellamy was baptized at thirteen, and sets into the glass the pledge as he wrote it, before the flag of the United States of America and before under God. The original twenty-three words survive in a Baptist church window in Oneida County, in coloured glass, in a version no schoolroom in the country has recited since 1924. The date of the window is not recorded anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The stained glass window at the First Baptist Church of Rome, bearing the 1892 text
sources: secondary aggregation citing the First Baptist Church of Rome

stops.name: New York, the great-granddaughter writes to the Times
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted; the coordinate is generic Manhattan and marks the newspaper, not the writer
stops.campa: With the two words of 1954 back in the federal courts, Sally Wright writes to the New York Times to say what her great-grandfather was: a deeply religious man and a strict believer in the separation of church and state, whose sentence was written to hold a country together and whose amendment, she argues, has divided it instead. The Smithsonian article that carried her account cannot be reached; the letter survives at one remove, through a secondary extraction, which is how most of this man reaches anyone.
stops.quote: My great-grandfather Francis Bellamy wrote the Pledge of Allegiance in 1892 for the widely read magazine Youth's Companion. A deeply religious man, he was also a strict believer in the separation of church and state...
stops.quote_source: Sally Wright, letter to the editor, New York Times, 2002, relayed via ushistory.org
suggested_refs: Sally Wright's 2002 letter to the New York Times on the 1954 amendment

stops.name: Hays, Kansas, another Bellamy
stops.date_confidence: circa 2022: a February 2022 date is given in one summary and could not be confirmed in any accessible source; the flag-raising the finding concerns is dated 30 April 1892
stops.campa: The amateur lexicographer Barry Popik surfaces a May 1892 Hays newspaper account of a school flag-raising held on the thirtieth of April, months before the Companion printed anything, at which children said an almost identical verse ending one nation inseparable. Reports credit a thirteen-year-old Kansas schoolboy named Frank E. Bellamy, no known relation. Fred Shapiro, who had credited Francis Bellamy in the Yale Book of Quotations, now says the evidence favours the boy. The dispute stands unsettled.
suggested_refs: The Hays, Kansas newspaper account of the flag-raising of 30 April 1892; the 1890 Youth's Companion patriotic competition
sources: reporting on the Barry Popik and Fred Shapiro research
